$comment: Corrections applied on top of the reference gir files. 'skip' removes symbols from generation, 'forceOpaque' keeps a record behind a pointer instead of copying it by value, 'rename' overrides the derived C# name, 'annotationOverrides' patches wrong or missing transfer/nullable/array annotations, 'returnTypeOverrides' narrows a returned handle onto the type that declares the member.
$comment-skip-static-str: The *_static_str family stores the string the caller passes by pointer and never copies it, so the string has to outlive every use of the object it was stored in. The generated marshalling hands native code a stack or heap buffer that is released when the call returns, which leaves the library holding a dangling pointer for every string that does not fit the short string optimisation. The gir carries no annotation that says a string must be static, so there is nothing for the planner to key on and the symbols are listed here. Binding them needs hand written glue that hands over an interned copy.
$comment-skip-identity: gst_buffer_remove_meta compares the GstMeta the caller passes by pointer identity against the metas of the buffer. The generated marshalling copies the structure into a local and passes the address of the copy, so the comparison never matches and the call silently removes nothing. Pointer identity is not something the gir states, so the symbol is listed here until hand written glue keeps the original address.
$comment-skip-annotations: These four functions carry annotations that do not describe what the C function does, and following them produces wrong lengths or wrong ownership: gst_adapter_map returns a pointer whose length is the size argument rather than an annotated array, gst_adapter_take returns freshly allocated memory of the size argument, gst_type_find_peek returns a borrowed pointer of the size argument, and gst_audio_ring_buffer_commit both reads and writes its sample count while its data pointer carries no length at all. An annotation override cannot add a missing array length, so they are skipped.
$comment-skip-consumed: gst_meta_info_register consumes the GstMetaInfo it is given and returns the registered one. The wrapper of an opaque record owns nothing and is never disposed, so nothing is freed twice, but the instance the caller still holds points at released memory the moment the call returns.
$comment-skip-superseded: gst_adapter_unmap releases what gst_adapter_map handed out, and gst_adapter_map is skipped just above. Emitting the release on its own leaves a public Unmap() with no Map() to pair it with, which unmaps a mapping the caller never took and releases a second time the one that the hand written scope holds. The mapping surface of an adapter is Gst.Base.Adapter.Map and the scope it returns, so this entry point is bound there and nowhere else.
$comment-skip-sync-handler: gst_bus_set_sync_handler installs a callback whose return value decides who owns the message: GST_BUS_DROP makes the handler responsible for unreffing it, every other reply leaves that to gst_bus_post. No annotation of the gir states a transfer that a return value turns on, so the generated marshalling cannot express it, and the emitted call had two faults because of it. It refused a null handler, which made the documented clear form unreachable and left a consumer unable to take the handler off at teardown; and its trampoline handed the managed handler a borrowed wrapper, so a handler that answered Drop leaked the reference of the poster with no way of consuming it from managed code. Both are fixed in Gst.Bus.SetSyncHandler and Gst.Bus.ClearSyncHandler, whose hand written trampoline drops that reference itself when the handler answers Drop. Skipping the call also retires the generated GstBusSyncHandler delegate, because the callback emitter only emits what a generated member takes, and the delegate is hand written next to the install so that its documentation can state the contract the binding actually implements.
$comment-skip-deinit: ges_deinit releases everything ges_init built, and the editing services are unusable until another ges_init. The binding runs ges_init from GstGES.Initialize, behind a latch that says it has run, and nothing in the library tells that latch when the resources are gone: a caller who takes the shut down of the process into their own hands leaves the entry point of the module reporting an initialised GES that no longer exists, and no call can bring it back. This is the shape gst_adapter_unmap has, a release with no acquisition of its own to pair with, and the same answer. Deinitialising GES is what ending the process does, which the documentation of the C function says as well.
$comment-force-opaque-sdp: The payload structures of an SDP message are plain C structures that the library hands out by pointer, and every accessor of theirs takes or returns such a pointer. A plain structure is projected as a value type, which copies it, and the methods declared on it are dropped for exactly that reason, so the media, attribute, origin, connection, bandwidth, time, zone and key surface of the module is unreachable. Keeping the eight of them behind a pointer binds it: the wrapper addresses the storage the message owns, so a read sees the message and a write reaches it. As on every other opaque record, 'Free' and 'Uninit' are public on the wrappers; neither may be called on an instance that a message still owns.
$comment-rename-get-type: gst_rtsp_message_get_type reads the message kind out of a GstRTSPMessage, and its derived C# name is GetType, which every object already declares. The generator refuses the collision and skips the member, so the kind of a message would be unreadable; GetMessageType is the name the C# surface gives it. The type of the record itself is registered under gst_rtsp_msg_get_type and is unaffected.
$comment-rename-commited: GESTimeline and GESTrack both emit their commit signal under the name 'commited', with one 't'. The typo is the API, since connecting to 'committed' connects to nothing, so the gir is right and only the C# name is corrected here. The signal name the generated code passes to GObject is the one of the gir; the rename reaches the event alone.
$comment-return-types: The gir spells the factory of a subclass with the return type of its base, so gst_pipeline_new returns a GstElement even though it only ever constructs a GstPipeline. The override narrows the wrapper onto the declaring type, which is the one the C implementation is known to build. The three network clock factories are the same shape with one wrinkle: gst_net_client_clock_new keeps a cache of clocks, which gst_net_client_clock_deinit is documented as clearing, so what it returns is not always freshly built. It is still an instance of the declaring type or of something below it, and the wrapper is created from the real type of the instance rather than from the declared one, so the narrowing holds either way.
